content:
According to Bloomberg, bipartisan US senators are urging Apple CEO Tim Cook to commit by August 21 not to use memory chips from Chinese suppliers CXMT (Changxin Memory Technologies) and YMTC (Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp). Here's the full story.

Background

Apple is looking for ways to address the ongoing memory chip shortage, and according to reports, the company has been seeking approval from the Trump administration to source components from CXMT and YMTC, which the US Department of Defense has designated as Chinese military companies.

Legally, Apple does not need US government approval to buy chips from these companies, but if it acts without the administration's backing, the company could face significant political consequences.

As a result, Apple CEO Tim Cook said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal just before the outlet's latest price hike that "all options should be on the table," adding, "we should consider all supply sources."

In the days that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple had been seeking assurances from the government that it would be allowed to purchase chips from CXMT, while the Financial Times reported Apple was in talks with YMTC to purchase chips. The Financial Times later reported that Apple was testing CXMT's DRAM chips.

Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple's use of Chinese memory chips may not be limited to the Chinese market, and that the company was seeking administration approval to use components from CXMT and YMTC in products sold outside the US.

The report also detailed that Micron was actively lobbying the government to reject Apple's request, on the grounds that allowing a Chinese supplier into Apple's supply chain could weaken domestic US memory production.

This isn't the first time Apple has tried to source memory chips from YMTC. In 2022, the company studied using components from the supplier in some iPhones sold in China, but the plan was shelved after it drew the attention of US lawmakers, as well as tightening export controls.

At the time, Senator Marco Rubio, who serves as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, accused Apple of "playing with fire," with other bipartisan lawmakers warning that the deal could pose a national security risk.

Lawmakers Renew Pressure

Bloomberg reported today that "a bipartisan group of US senators is urging Apple to abandon any move to source chips from blacklisted Chinese semiconductor suppliers [CXMT] and [YMTC], warning the iPhone maker risks relying on a US-adversary nation for critical components."

According to the report, lawmakers called Apple's plans "short-sighted" and said the move would "ensure that the world's most valuable consumer electronics company becomes increasingly dependent on a supplier formally designated by the US government as a Chinese military company for critical components."

Lawmakers also argued that other companies might follow Apple's lead, potentially undermining domestic US memory production, as well as planned investments in states such as Indiana, Idaho, New York, and Virginia.

They added that any initial restriction limiting CXMT memory chips to use in products sold in China would be hard to maintain, since "once a component has been through Apple's production certification, rolling it out for global use is just a procurement decision away."

Finally, in addition to demanding that Apple commit by August 21 to "avoid the use of CXMT or YMTC memory in its products," the senators also requested that Apple provide details on any data shared with CXMT during the component certification process, noting that transferring controlled technical data to advanced Chinese chipmaking facilities may require Commerce Department approval.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
